interest: For historians, this collection offers an intimate, real-time chronicle of the decisive breakdown of civilian parliamentary authority and the consolidation of military ascendancy in prewar Japan. It is especially valuable for preserving primary rebel manifestos, detailed secret court-martial proceedings, and immediate regional reactions—such as candid assessments by Chinese leaders Dr. H. H. Kung and T. V. Soong on Japan's expanding imperial ambitions. Additionally, the records shed crucial light on both domestic resistance to militarism—highlighted by Takao Saito's defiant Diet address—and the structural mechanics of the Army's political power, most notably demonstrated by its refusal to nominate a War Minister in order to torpedo General Ugaki's cabinet formation.
overview: This file documents the internal political crises, foreign policy trajectories, and accelerating militarization of Japan from the immediate aftermath of the February 26, 1936 military coup d'état through the installation of the Hayashi Cabinet in early 1937. Through diplomatic despatches from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and U.S. consular posts, military intelligence reports, and State Department memoranda, the collection traces the judicial and political handling of the rebellion—including the court-martial trials and executions of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa and young rebel officers, as well as the termination of Tokyo martial law. It chronicles the short-lived Hirota Cabinet as it capitulated to Army demands for vast national defense budgets, state-directed economic controls, and ideological suppression via the surveillance of 'dangerous thoughts,' alongside inter-service strategic debates balancing the Navy's 'southward advance' (Nanshin-ron) against the Army's continental ambitions. The file culminates in the January 1937 parliamentary crisis, sparked by bitter clashes in the Diet between party politicians and War Minister Terauchi, leading to the collapse of the Hirota government, the Army's unprecedented veto blocking General Kazushige Ugaki from the premiership, and the establishment of General Senjuro Hayashi's transitional, military-aligned administration.
